title: The $30,000 Intro: Contingency Recruiting Math (November 2026)
summary: Contingency recruiters charge 15-30% of salary, turning one intro into a $30,000 bill. Here's the math and a cheaper path for startups (November 2026).
body_markdown:
Startups that have outgrown their network face three options: source candidates alone, build a recruiting team from scratch, or pay an external recruiter on contingency. The contingency route looks risk-free because payment only follows a hire, yet its pricing can turn a single introduction into a[$30,000 fee](https://www.dover.com/) . Understanding where that fee comes from, and how it shapes the candidates a recruiter sends, makes it easier to judge when contingency fits and when a retained or hourly model costs less.


**TLDR:**


- Contingency recruiters typically charge 15-25% of first-year base salary, rising to 25-30% for senior or specialist roles, so a $150k engineer hire can cost about $30,000.
- That pricing is built to cover losses on unsuccessful searches, beyond the cost of the one search that succeeds.
- Because the contingency model pays a recruiter when a candidate gets hired anywhere, the incentive favors speed and resume volume over candidate fit.
- Flat monthly retainers or hourly models charge fees closer to the direct cost of the search, which can better align incentives with the hiring company.
- Contingency can still suit an urgent, one-off hire where speed matters more than cost control.


## The Economics of Contingency Recruiting


As a founder or hiring manager at a growing startup, a huge portion of your time is dedicated to finding the best people for your team. You’ve made your first few hires from your network and from referrals,[but after about 10 to 15 hires,](https://medium.com/@jmtame/surprising-insights-from-talking-to-hiring-teams-in-silicon-valley-e8f06b8f9aa) you start to exhaust your network.


At this point, you have a few options. You can source candidates yourself, but even with the abundance of tools out there, it will be tedious and time-consuming. You can also start building out a recruiting team, but this comes with its own challenges: starting a recruiting search from scratch will take months, and you still won’t be any closer to making the key hires you initially sought.


The third option is to[partner with an external recruiter](https://www.dover.com/blog/startup-agency-recruiting-vs-recruiter-marketplace) . However, most of the time, misaligned incentives drive up recruiting fees many times over the actual cost of the hire.


## How Contingency and Retained Recruiting Work


Since you need to make these hires quickly and don’t have time to do it yourself, you decide to work with an agency. Agencies work on either a[retained or a contingency basis](https://www.indeed.com/hire/c/info/contingency-retained-recruiting) : “contingency” means you only pay when you hire one of their candidates, while traditional “retained” search is paid in installments that start when the search begins, usually tied to the hire’s salary. Some recruiters also offer a flat monthly retainer instead, and that’s the model this post compares against contingency.


On the surface, it seems like the incentives are much more aligned in the contingency model. You don’t have to pay until you make a hire, so it’s essentially risk-free.


You reach out to one of your VCs and get a referral for a recruiter named Dave. After a 30 minute meeting with Dave, you enter a contingency agreement with him.


## Under the Hood of a Contingency Search


Dave helps companies in San Francisco hire senior engineers, and over the years, he’s set up contingency agreements with a few dozen startups. He reaches out to engineers every day, checks in with his old connections to see if they’re ready for a job change, and tries to have a few phone calls a day to pitch new candidates on his companies.


The engineers he targets have an average salary of $150k, and Dave charges a 20% contingency fee, so he makes $30k if he succeeds in filling a role. Current[recruiter fee benchmarks](https://boostpoint.com/recruiter-cost/) put contingency rates at 15-25% of first-year base salary, rising to 25-30% for senior or specialist roles. Here’s why it’s so expensive:


- Contingency recruiters are a company’s last resort. By the time a company brings on Dave, they’ve often already tapped referrals, inbound interest, job boards, and other contingency recruiters. They likely already have a couple of candidates in active conversations, and may hire one of them shortly after contracting with Dave.
- Contingency recruiters upcharge to cover their losses on other searches. Dave is lucky if one in three searches he conducts leads to a hire. Since he’s only successful a third of the time, Dave needs to charge three times as much as it costs to fill a role. Each search costs Dave $10k to run. If he wastes $20k of his time working on two unsuccessful searches, he’ll need to charge $30k to recuperate his losses.


With these dynamics in mind, we can start to see the real incentives at play.


## Misaligned Incentives


After entering the contingency agreement with Dave, you start to receive candidate resumes. Every day you get a handful to review, and a couple of trends stand out.


Most of the candidates that Dave is sending are a poor fit and are low quality. You send Dave some feedback and send him the job description again to remind him of what you’re looking for in this hire. But little changes over the subsequent weeks.


Once in a while, Dave sends over a candidate that matches what you’re looking for. You tell Dave to make the intro, but you find out that the candidate is already interviewing with four other companies and that you need to move extremely quickly.


You’re experiencing this for a couple of reasons:


- You’re not the contingency recruiter’s customer. The candidate is. The contingency model pays Dave when his candidates get hired, regardless of which company hires them. In fact, when Dave finally finds a strong, active candidate, it makes sense for him to introduce that candidate to[each and every one of his companies](https://www.dover.com/blog/dedicated-vs-multi-recruiter-hiring-model) .
- For the contingency recruiter, speed is more important than quality. Dave is in a race against you, as you might fill your role through another channel. He’s also in a race against the candidates he’s working with, as all of them are also looking for jobs through other means. As a result, Dave will make sacrifices on quality of the candidate fit and company fit in the interest of speed.
- The contingency recruiter just needs to find *a* candidate, not the *best* candidate. Dave wants to take more shots on goal by sending you as many resumes as possible. Even if each candidate is not a great fit, he doesn’t lose anything by introducing them to you.


After sifting through dozens of resumes and interviewing many candidates, Dave introduces you to a reasonable candidate. After hiring the candidate, Dave sends you a bill for $30,000. You pay Dave, but the fee feels steep given the outcome. He found you a mediocre candidate, and you still ended up doing much of the work to hire them yourself.


The problem with contingency recruiting is that misaligned incentives drive up the cost.


## What Contingency Fees Look Like in 2026


According to[SHRM’s 2025 Benchmarking Report](https://www.shrm.org/about/press-room/shrm-releases-2025-benchmarking-reports--how-does-your-organizat) , the average non-executive cost per hire is $5,475, and SHRM’s[2026 recruiting benchmarking update](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/research/recruiting-benchmarking) reports that non-executive costs held relatively steady. A $30,000 contingency fee on a $150k engineer hire is more than five times that average, which helps explain why founders often feel the sting when the invoice arrives.


Recruiter pricing today commonly spans contingency, retained search, and[hourly fractional recruiting](https://www.dover.com/blog/fractional-recruiting-employers-guide) , giving founders more ways to pay for the work actually done instead of a flat percentage of salary. Contingency can still make sense for an urgent, one-off hire where speed matters more than cost control, but it is worth weighing the alternatives before signing an agreement.


## An Alternative Path


Moving from the contingency model to a flat monthly retainer can correct for these misaligned incentives. Imagine if you had hired Stacy, a recruiter paid a flat monthly retainer. This differs from traditional retained executive search, which is usually priced as a percentage of salary. Her incentives will be better aligned with your own:


- You would be Stacy’s customer, not the candidates.
- Stacy wouldn’t be incentivized to send you low-quality candidates.
- Stacy could charge a fee that’s more in line with the direct cost of working for you, $10k.


*Contingency vs. flat-retainer recruiting on a $150k engineering hire*


Factor Contingency (Dave) Flat retainer (Stacy)


How you pay Only when you hire one of their candidates Fixed monthly fee


Who the recruiter works for The candidate You


Incentive Speed and volume of resumes Candidate fit for your role


Fee on this hire $30,000, 20% of $150k salary About $10,000, the direct cost of the search


Pricing covers Losses on unsuccessful searches The work done for you


The best way to reduce the cost of recruiting is to create the right incentive structure. A flat retainer may not be perfect for all cases, but it will change your expenses from the expected cost to the[actual cost of the search](https://www.dover.com/blog/fractional-recruitment-agency-guide) .


A retained or hourly recruiter also tends to work better when the recruiter and hiring team share one applicant tracking system, since both sides see the same pipeline in real time. Without a shared system, recruiters often track candidates in their own tools, and that history may leave with them when the engagement ends.


## How Dover Fits Into Fractional Recruiting


Dover’s model is built around the incentive problem described above. It pairs a free applicant tracking system with a marketplace of fractional recruiters who bill by the hour, so the fee follows the work done and not the salary of the person hired. A recruiter has no financial reason to push a higher-paid candidate or to send the same resume to every client.


Each recruiter on the marketplace sets their own rate, and the average cost per hire across all roles is about $4,800, though costs vary by role seniority and hiring complexity. On the $150k engineering hire used in this example, that sits well below the contingency fee. Recruiters on the marketplace can also work on a retainer or a pay-per-hire basis, which keeps contingency available for an urgent, one-off search.


Recruiters can work inside the company’s own ATS or in existing tools such as Ashby, Greenhouse, or Lever. When they use the company’s own ATS, candidate notes and outreach history stay with the company after an engagement ends, and each search builds on the last. Intro calls are free, a refundable deposit opens access to the marketplace, and there are no long-term contracts, so a team can pause or switch recruiters anytime.


## FAQs


### How much does a contingency recruiter charge?


Contingency fees typically run 15-25% of a candidate’s first-year base salary, with rates often climbing to 25-30% for senior or specialist roles. You only pay when the recruiter’s candidate gets hired, but the percentage can make the final bill far larger than a founder expects going in.


### When does contingency recruiting make sense?


Contingency recruiting tends to work best for an urgent, one-off hire where speed matters more than cost control. If you need a single role filled quickly and don’t plan to run a long-term search, the risk-free structure can outweigh the higher fee.


### Is a retained recruiter always cheaper?


Not always. Traditional retained search is often priced as a percentage of salary and can cost as much as contingency, or more. A flat monthly retainer or hourly arrangement ties pay to the work done, which can lower costs over several hires but may cost more if a single search stalls.


### Do I need an ATS before bringing in a fractional recruiter?


An ATS isn’t strictly required, but it typically makes a fractional engagement run more cleanly. The ATS handles job posting, applicant tracking, and interview scheduling, while the recruiter adds sourcing and screening capacity on top of it. When the recruiter works inside the company’s own ATS, candidate records stay with the company after the engagement ends. Free options exist, including Dover’s ATS, which pairs with on-demand fractional recruiters.


## Final Thoughts on Contingency Recruiting Fees and Choosing a Hiring Model


Contingency pricing builds the cost of every unsuccessful search into the one that succeeds, which is how a single introduction ends up carrying a $30,000 fee. The right model depends on hiring volume, urgency, and how much control a team wants over the search, and contingency remains reasonable for a one-off role where speed outweighs cost. For teams hiring across several roles, a structure that charges for the work done tends to line the recruiter’s incentives up with the company’s, and Dover’s fractional model, which pairs a free ATS with on-demand recruiters, is one example of that approach.
